books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: “Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all,” broadside, April 24, 1851

stimulus.source_note: “Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all,” broadside posted in Boston, April 24, 1851 (Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection). Public domain.
stimulus.text: Caution!! Colored people of Boston, one & all, You are hereby respectfully cautioned and advised, to avoid conversing with the Watchmen and Police Officers of Boston, For since the recent Order of the Mayor & Aldermen, they are empowered to act as Kidnappers and Slave Catchers, And they have already been actually employed in Kidnapping, Catching, and Keeping Slaves. Therefore, if you value your Liberty, and the Welfare of the Fugitives among you, Shun them in every possible manner, as so many Hounds on the track of the most unfortunate of your race. Keep a Sharp Look Out for Kidnappers, and have Top Eye open. April 24, 1851.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The broadside is best used as evidence that the Fugitive Slave Act

options.text: changed daily life for free Black Northerners, not only for runaways.
was welcomed in Boston as a fair settlement of the slavery question.
options.misconception: A warning broadside is not a welcome; it tells Black Bostonians their liberty is in danger from the law.

options.text: applied only to people who had escaped from slavery after 1850.
options.misconception: The broadside warns all Black Bostonians, not only recent escapees. Background from the books: under the act, a claimant's sworn affidavit was enough to start a seizure, so even free Black Northerners were at risk.
Background from the books: the act was enforced in Boston — Shadrach Minkins was seized there in February 1851, and Thomas Sims was returned to slavery that April.

rationales.A: The warning speaks to “Colored people of Boston, one & all” — every Black Bostonian, free or fugitive — telling them to shun the police as “Hounds on the track of the most unfortunate of your race.”
rationales.B: A warning broadside is not a welcome; it tells Black Bostonians their liberty is in danger from the law.
rationales.C: The broadside warns all Black Bostonians, not only recent escapees. Background from the books: under the act, a claimant's sworn affidavit was enough to start a seizure, so even free Black Northerners were at risk.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the act was enforced in Boston — Shadrach Minkins was seized there in February 1851, and Thomas Sims was returned to slavery that April.
rationales.general:
1. Notice who the broadside addresses: “Colored people of Boston, one & all,” not only runaways.
2. Ask what it tells them to fear: not a court far away, but the policeman on their own street.
3. See the law's reach: it turned free Black Northerners into people who had to watch every conversation.
Remember: the best evidence of a law's effect is often a warning posted on a wall, not a speech in Congress.
